messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Retail Worker
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 59

He is a 36-year-old European man who has been married for nine years and works in retail, a job that once suited him because it kept him busy and around people without asking too much of him. Before the event, he describes himself as steady and practical, someone who could handle long shifts, crowded stores, and the ordinary stress of customers and deadlines. That changed after the man-made disaster at the shopping center where he was working one evening, when a sudden, violent crisis unfolded in a place that had always felt familiar and routine.

He remembers the moments before it happened as unremarkable: folding merchandise, answering a question from a customer, thinking about dinner with his wife. Then everything shifts. There is shouting, running, the sharp sound of panic spreading faster than anyone can understand it. He is not prepared for the terror in the room, for the confusion of not knowing what is happening or what direction is safe. He describes the scene in fragments—broken glass, people crying out, the metallic taste of fear, his own body moving before his mind can catch up. In the aftermath, he is left with the awful knowledge that a normal day at work has been transformed into something he cannot get out of his head.

In the first weeks afterward, he tries to return to his routine because he believes that is what he should do. He goes back to work, but the store no longer feels ordinary. Loud noises make him flinch. A dropped display or a sudden customer complaint can send a surge of panic through him. He scans entrances automatically, tracks exits without thinking, and positions himself where he can see the whole floor. He notices himself becoming irritable and tense, snapping at coworkers and then feeling ashamed. At home, he is present in body but often elsewhere in his mind, drifting into replaying the event or bracing for something bad to happen. His wife says he seems distant, and he cannot fully explain that being close to her sometimes makes him feel guilty, as though he is failing at being the calm husband he used to be.

As time goes on, the memories become more intrusive rather than less. He is startled by sirens, construction noise, or even the sudden slam of a car door. He has nightmares that wake him in the early morning with his heart pounding, though the details slip away as soon as he opens his eyes. During the day, he experiences unwanted images of the disaster when he least expects them—standing at a register, driving, or hearing a raised voice in public. He finds himself avoiding shopping centers, crowded spaces, and news coverage of violent events. Even at work, he takes longer routes through the store, avoids the section where the incident began, and feels a surge of dread if he is asked to stay late. He does not say these things out loud at first, but his body tells the story: muscle tension, shallow breathing, an exhausted vigilance that never really lets him rest.

He also struggles with a persistent sense that the world is less safe than it once seemed. He used to think of himself as competent and resilient, but now he often feels on edge, as if danger could break through at any moment. He checks locks repeatedly at home and has trouble falling asleep because his mind keeps rehearsing possible threats. When he does sleep, it is light and broken. Concentration is harder at work, and he catches himself rereading labels or losing track of customer requests. He hates that he feels so easily rattled. More than once, he has thought that others must notice how jumpy he has become, and that thought makes him withdraw further.

Over time, he becomes quieter with friends and less willing to make plans. He tells himself he is just tired, but the truth is that he does not trust his own reactions. He worries that if something happens again, he will freeze or fail to protect the people near him. That fear sits beneath much of his daily life, shaping the way he moves through work, home, and public places. Even in moments of relative calm, he remains alert, as though waiting for the next disruption.
